newsitem.title: INDIA: India policymaker calls for dropping import curbs.
newsitem.headline: India policymaker calls for dropping import curbs.

text.p: A leading Indian policymaker said on Wednesday the country could face punitive action if it did not ease import restrictions as demanded by other member countries of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"We are on a weak wicket and we don't have any other option but to amend our laws," G.V. Ramakrishna, chairman of the government-appointed Disinvestment Commission said at a Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (ASSOCHAM) seminar.

"If the WTO rules against India, which it is most likely to, then there could be systematic punitive action ranging from import restrictions to tariff hikes and other such measures," Ramakrishna said.
He said India stood accused in complaints filed in the WTO by the United States, Japan, the European Union and some other countries, including Australia, New Zealand and Canada.
The major trade powers are protesting against India's decades-old import restrictions. They argue the Indian measures run against WTO open trading accords.

Last week Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah said India was confident of resolving the issue amicably. He said India had already reduced the timeframe for removing quantitative restrictions on imports to six years from an earlier proposal for nine years, and would stick to what it had said.

The restrictions, which affect some 2,700 items ranging from consumer goods to agricultural products, have been in force since the 1950s, but were accepted by other countries because of India's earlier endemic balance-of-payments problems.
But with steady growth in the country's foreign exchange reserves, which reached $28.8 billion in June, other WTO members have insisted Delhi agree to move quickly to drop curbs.

The United States was reportedly pressing for a three year phase-out of restrictions, while the EU and other WTO members indicated an acceptance of a five year period if limits on most big-ticket items were removed early on.
Under the WTO's dispute settlement procedure, India must respond to the requests for consultations within 10 days and start them within 20 days.
If two months pass without a solution, the complaining countries can ask the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body to set up a panel to rule on the issue.
Meanwhile Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Wednesday that disputes should be settled mutually. "Before going to the dispute panel we should try to resolve the issue bilaterally," he said.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted visiting Australian Finance Minister Alexander Downer as saying the issue of quantitative restrictions by India could be settled without going to the WTO.
"There is a point of disagreement on it at the moment and we hope to conclude it through negotiations in the next few weeks," PTI quoted Downer as saying.
Australia is one of the countries which has referred the matter to the dispute settlement body of the WTO.
